title: The ladder of names
hook: Dionysius the Areopagite: God beyond names, beyond being

segments.voice: Yesterday, Boethius in prison, and Philosophy sitting on the edge of his bed. Your line was the wheel turns. What went up or down for you, and what stayed put? Day one thousand two hundred forty-five.

At the very end of a chapter in Acts, after a speech, comes a short list of the people who stayed behind: "Howbeit certain men clave unto him, and believed: among the which was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them." That's all the Bible tells us about him. A name in a list. The speech he heard had started from an altar with no god's name on it, and Paul read its inscription aloud: "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you." Later, a set of writings appeared under this listener's name, and they go straight back to that altar. They ask whether not knowing God's name could be where wisdom starts.

The texts claim the name of that listener from Acts. Modern scholars generally read them as written much later by an unknown author, and call him Pseudo-Dionysius; Orthodox tradition still honors them under the name Dionysius. What they teach is a ladder, and it runs in two directions. Going down the ladder, you name God. Scripture gives plenty of names: good, light, life, wisdom, love. In a book called The Divine Names, Dionysius treats them one by one, and says each is true. God really is good. God really is light. Then comes the climb back up, and it runs the other way. Now you take the names off, one at a time, starting from the lowest. God is not a rock, not a fire, not a king the way kings are kings. Keep climbing, and you take off even the high names. God is not good the way we know good, not even being the way things are. Not because God is less, but because God is beyond. Dionysius says God is both the one with many names and the nameless one. At the top of the ladder there's no more talking. He points to Moses on the mountain. Exodus says: "Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was." A darkness, Dionysius says, that's actually too much light. This way of speaking is called apophatic: speaking of God by saying what God is not. Eastern Orthodox theology makes much of it, and Western mystics drew on it too. And it gave Christians a kind of humility in words: every name is true, and every name falls short.
screen: `UP THE LADDER: TAKE THE NAMES OFF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with God beyond words. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, start with one name you use for God: Father, Lord, light, love. Say it once, slowly, inside. Then let even that word go quiet, and stay in the space it pointed toward, without filling it. If you don't pray, choose a word for whatever is biggest to you and do the same. Whenever a new word rushes in, notice it, and set it down. The bell holds the time.
The ladder of names. Name God from scripture going down; take the names off going up, until there's only the thick darkness where God was.
Your line: beyond every name. Today, when you catch yourself sure you've got someone figured out, a person or God, add quietly: and more than that. Day one thousand two hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Eastern Orthodox Christians in particular speak of the apophatic way, approaching God by saying what God is not; Christians of different churches practice wordless prayer in the same spirit.

original.note: Greek: denial, saying no. apophatic speech speaks of God by saying what God is not.

what it means: on Dionysius's ladder, you name God from scripture, then take the names off one by one, because God is beyond them all.
what a scholar hears: the writings claim the name of Paul's convert in Acts 17:34; modern scholars read them as much later, so they say Pseudo-Dionysius.

notes: Dionysius is paraphrased throughout. Check: God as 'of many names' and 'nameless' (Divine Names 1); affirmations descending from the highest, negations ascending from the lowest (Mystical Theology 2–3); Moses entering the darkness (Mystical Theology 1.3); the 'darkness' as beyond light.
Authorship: the script says only that it is 'an open question' and that 'some readers' say Pseudo-Dionysius; no date given by design. Confirm.
'Some mock him ... but some stay and believe' paraphrases Acts 17:32–34 (some mocked, others would hear again, certain men clave unto him); confirm.
'Eastern Orthodox Christians call this way of speaking apophatic' and 'Western mystics drew on it too' are general statements; confirm. Greek ἀπόφασις: accent and pronunciation to check.
Acts 17:23 KJV prints the inscription in capitals; preserved.

Editor pass: day 1237 (Justin) already opened on Paul's speech in Athens, so the hook now starts from Acts 17:34, the list naming Dionysius (quoted, KJV), and reaches the altar second; cut the 'some mock him' paraphrase. Cut the spoken etymology of apophatic ('from a Greek word for saying no') under the claims rule; the original game keeps the Greek word's meaning but no longer calls it 'the root'.

Audit (2026-10-02): authorship was framed as 'an open question' with 'some readers' saying Pseudo-Dionysius, which understates the modern scholarly consensus that the corpus is much later than the Acts figure; now says modern scholars generally read it as later and that Orthodox tradition still honors it under the name Dionysius (no date given). 'Eastern Orthodox Christians call this apophatic' reworded: the term is used across churches. Confirm.
